title: A cop's case for Flock  - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: A serving police officer defends Flock Safety's cheap automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) cameras against a sudden nationwide backlash, arguing the technology measurably raises crime-solving rates, comes with audit protections, and has withstood Fourth Amendment court challenges. He concedes real abuse cases exist but argues the cameras will persist regardless because rivals and private buyers can deploy identical systems.

insights.claim: Flock Safety, an Atlanta startup founded in 2017, sells solar-powered roadside ALPR cameras that photograph passing cars, read plates, and instantly check them against the FBI's national database of stolen cars and wanted persons, alerting nearby officers on a match.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Defines the product and its real-time alerting edge, the basis for its rapid police-market penetration.

insights.claim: Flock undercut legacy ALPR by pricing a more accurate camera at a $3,000 annual subscription against a typical US police department's $1 million budget, and now roughly 30 percent of US police agencies subscribe.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Cheap subscription pricing drove near-ubiquitous adoption, a textbook land-grab that also created the political surface area for backlash.
insights.quote: Flock’s idea was to sell a more accurate ALPR camera for an annual subscription of just $3,000
insights.locator: For much of the technology’s history

insights.claim: Flock does not have a monopoly: at least five other companies offer almost identical ALPR products to public and private buyers, some arguably more invasive, and some cities canceling Flock contracts have signed up with its rivals.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Backlash targeting one brand doesn't shrink the ALPR market; demand simply migrates to competitors, a key point for anyone assessing the sector.
insights.locator: Flock did not invent its capabilities

insights.claim: American police solve only 8.2 percent of reported vehicle thefts with an arrest, but a working paper found agencies adopting ALPR saw a 15.9 percent relative increase in car thefts caught, which would raise the national rate to 9.5 percent.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Quantifies the efficacy claim with a working-paper figure, the empirical core of the pro-Flock case.
insights.quote: agencies that adopted the devices saw a 15.9 percent relative increase in car thefts caught
insights.locator: Stolen cars provide the clearest evidence

insights.claim: After Atlantic City expanded its ALPR network, monthly motor vehicle thefts dropped 20 percent, property crimes 34 percent, and fatal shootings by almost 40 percent, with 72 alert-caused stops locating 40 stolen vehicles and nine stolen plates.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A city-level natural experiment showing broad crime reduction beyond car theft, strengthening the deployment case.

insights.claim: Flock's own study claims 10 percent of all reported crime in the United States is solved using evidence from its cameras.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A striking but company-sourced statistic, useful to note as vendor-marketing signal rather than independent evidence.
insights.quote: 10 percent of all reported crime in the United States is solved using evidence obtained from their cameras

insights.claim: ALPR has a decades-long track record: a 1976 British Home Office invention, first ALPR arrest in 1981, and 2004's Project Laser read over five million plates yielding 3,071 arrests, later praised as the best investigative tool since DNA analysis.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Establishes the technology as mature and validated, countering framing of Flock as a novel or untested threat.

insights.claim: More than 150 cities and towns have deactivated Flock cameras or canceled contracts within weeks, some despite their own audits finding no officer misuse, with opposition spanning from Bernie Sanders to Knox County's Republican mayor Kane.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Documents a fast, bipartisan reputational collapse, a governance risk that can reverse an adoption curve regardless of efficacy data.

insights.claim: The author argues Flock's core structural problem is that success is invisible: a crime deterred produces no victim or report, while every misuse yields a victim and a corrupt-cop mugshot and every false alert an image of an innocent motorist in handcuffs.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: An asymmetry-of-evidence framework explaining why surveillance tech is politically fragile even when net-beneficial, a reusable lens for regulatory-risk assessment.
insights.quote: if it works, it provides no visible benefits outside the crime statistics
insights.locator: The problem for Flock is that

insights.claim: Flock includes accountability controls: every search requires a recorded reason and case number published in monthly audits, plate retention was cut from thirty days to seven, and algorithms plus audits flag suspicious searches and block users pending senior review.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The audit architecture is the author's rebuttal to abuse claims and the differentiator versus unaudited manual surveillance.

insights.claim: The Institute for Justice, an ALPR critic, found 51 Flock-misuse incidents across the US since 2024 and noted that nearly all those officers were criminally charged and lost their jobs.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Even a critic's data shows abuse is rare and consequences enforced, a key counter to the abuse-with-impunity narrative.
insights.quote: Nearly all of these officers were criminally charged and lost their jobs, either by resigning or getting fired
insights.locator: The Institute for Justice, a think tank

insights.claim: Flock cannot search for individuals, identify who is driving a scanned vehicle, or scan phones and devices, and an officer must independently establish who is behind the wheel before gaining probable cause to stop a flagged car.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Clarifies the technology's actual limits against exaggerated claims, material for calibrating regulatory and civil-liberties debate.

insights.claim: Courts have repeatedly upheld ALPR: the Supreme Court held unanimously in 1983 that a person on public thoroughfares has no reasonable expectation of privacy in their movements, and a January 2026 federal judge in Virginia ruled that scanning a license plate invades no privacy interest.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Strong legal precedent makes a nationwide ALPR ban unlikely, capping the regulatory downside for the technology's providers.
insights.quote: An individual scan of a license plate, a vehicle identifier that generally must be displayed under state law, does not invade any privacy interests

insights.claim: The author predicts a divergent patchwork of local ALPR policies rather than a ban, and that cameras won't disappear because the Fourth Amendment binds only government, letting homeowners associations buy their own Flock networks.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Private-market deployment is the escape valve that keeps ALPR growing even where public agencies retreat, a durability thesis for the sector.
insights.locator: It seems unlikely that America will ever ban ALPR

insights.claim: The author argues the biggest losers from Flock restrictions are residents of average small towns, since almost 50 percent of US police departments employ fewer than ten officers and cannot afford helicopters, drones, or enough officers to watch every road.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Frames ALPR as a force-multiplier for under-resourced small departments, the distributional argument at the heart of the pro-Flock case.
insights.quote: almost 50 percent of the country’s police departments employ fewer than ten full-time officers
